summary: Describes the authors' experience building a SOAP-based NETCONF client and server. It describes an alternative SOAP binding that does not interoperate with an implementation following RFC 4743, and discusses how existing SOAP tools can reduce development effort. This is an informational document.

plainLanguage.summary: Some people built a tool for managing network gear by using ready-made software parts. They wrote down what they learned, including one place where their version wouldn't work with the official one.

subtitle: Building network management systems by layering NETCONF on SOAP and using standard development tools

tldr.problem: Developers needed practical experience and guidelines for implementing NETCONF (network configuration protocol) over SOAP, including how to leverage existing development tools to reduce effort.
tldr.mechanism: The document describes an implementation architecture using SOAP over HTTP with Java-based development tools (Apache Axis, WSDL generation), where automatic code generation from WSDL files eliminates the need to write SOAP directly.
tldr.outcome: Developers can build NETCONF clients and servers using standard Web Services tools and approaches, though the authors' implementation uses HTTP cookies and does not interoperate with RFC 4743 compliant systems.

today: RFC 5381 is an informational document describing implementation experience. It is not a standard and does not interoperate with RFC 4743 compliant implementations due to its use of HTTP cookies. However, it remains valuable as a guide to practical NETCONF development using Web Services tools.

sections.title: NETCONF as a Web Service
sections.content:
NETCONF (Network Configuration Protocol) was specified in RFC 4741 as the standard way to configure network equipment. RFC 4743 added SOAP (Simple Object Access Protocol) as an optional transport for NETCONF, allowing it to work like a Web Service. Because SOAP is already well integrated into development tools and frameworks, developers hoped using SOAP would make building network management systems faster and cheaper.

This RFC documents the implementation experience of engineers at Alaxala Networks and Hitachi who built both a NETCONF client (an NMS, or Network Management System) and a NETCONF server (running on network equipment) using SOAP. Rather than hand-coding NETCONF and SOAP messages, they generated Java code automatically from WSDL (Web Services Description Language) and XSD (XML Schema Definition) files. The document explains the architecture, implementation decisions, and practical guidelines they developed, including where their approach diverges from RFC 4743.
sections.plainLanguage: Network equipment needs to be configured. SOAP is a standard way computers talk to each other. These engineers used standard tools to make it work, and they wrote down what they learned.

sections.title: Web Services Framework and Code Generation
sections.content:
Web Services combine several standards: XML for data description, WSDL for service interface definition, SOAP for messaging, and standard transport (typically HTTP). At the center is SOAP, which defines how messages are structured. WSDL files describe what messages a service accepts and returns, allowing tools to automatically generate the APIs needed to use the service.

The key insight is that once you have a WSDL file, development tools like Apache Axis can generate complete Java libraries (stubs) that encapsulate all SOAP details. A developer using these libraries never writes XML or SOAP directly; they call simple Java methods like getConfig() or editConfig(), and the library handles serialization and network transport. This dramatically reduces both the learning curve and the code developers must write. The authors describe using WSDL files from RFC 4741 (NETCONF) and RFC 4743 (NETCONF over SOAP) as the starting point.
sections.plainLanguage: WSDL is a recipe that describes what messages to send. Tools like Apache Axis read the recipe and automatically write all the tricky code that sends and receives messages.

sections.title: Client and Server Implementation Architecture
sections.content:
The architecture divides the system into layers. The NETCONF application layer (running in the NMS on the client side, or as a network service provider on the server side) deals only with NETCONF messages and configurations. Below it sits automatically generated Java library code that translates NETCONF operations into SOAP messages. At the bottom, a SOAP implementation (Apache Axis in the NMS, or a similar SOAP library on network equipment) handles XML parsing and HTTP transport.

On the client side, the NMS uses Apache Axis to parse SOAP responses, maintain NETCONF sessions, and send NETCONF requests wrapped in SOAP over HTTP. The authors note that HTTP is stateless, so they used HTTP cookies (stored in HTTP headers) to associate incoming requests with stored NETCONF session identifiers. This differs from RFC 4743, which ties session state to the underlying TCP connection. On the server side, network equipment must also run a SOAP implementation, though they mention memory constraints might require simplified SOAP parsers that skip optional SOAP headers to reduce footprint.
sections.plainLanguage: The client side has the management tool, which talks through generated code and SOAP to network equipment. The equipment side has similar layers. Cookies help keep track of which conversation is which.

sections.title: Development Procedures for NETCONF Clients and Servers
sections.content:
For clients, the authors recommend using WSDL2Java (a tool in Apache Axis) to generate stub files from the NETCONF WSDL files. The command specifies the WSDL location and an output package, and generates Java files like NetconfBindingStub.java, Netconf.java, and type files like EditConfigType.java. These generated files are then compiled and used as libraries. Developers extend the stubs to add application logic (such as logging, error handling, or the specific network configurations they want to deploy).

Using an IDE like Eclipse with Apache Ant build automation simplifies this further. Configuration files build.xml and build.properties define the build process once, allowing a single Ant command to generate stubs, compile, and package everything into a JAR library. The authors note that proper UTF-8 encoding settings in the compilation step are important for international compatibility. For server-side development, the process is similar but the generated code implements NETCONF service providers that handle incoming requests; the authors also briefly mention developing servers in the C programming language for systems where Java is not available.
sections.plainLanguage: To build a client: use a tool to turn the WSDL recipe into Java code, write the logic you want, and compile. IDEs like Eclipse make this even easier by automating all the steps.

sections.title: Practical Implementation Notes
sections.content:
The session maintenance mechanism used cookies placed in HTTP headers to map requests to NETCONF sessions. After the NMS sends a NETCONF hello (introduction) message, the network equipment's NETCONF service provider assigns a session ID, includes it in the reply's NETCONF <session> element, and also places it in an HTTP Set-Cookie header. The NMS stores this ID and includes it in all subsequent NETCONF requests and HTTP Cookie headers. This approach works over HTTP's stateless nature but creates an incompatibility with RFC 4743 implementations that rely on TCP connection state instead.

The document also notes memory constraints on network equipment: SOAP parsers can be simplified to parse only mandatory parts of SOAP envelopes (skipping optional SOAP headers) to reduce memory footprint. By carefully choosing lightweight SOAP libraries and avoiding unnecessary features, the authors successfully deployed NETCONF management on devices with limited resources. This combination of standard tools (WSDL, SOAP, HTTP, cookies) and practical optimizations made NETCONF over SOAP viable on a range of equipment and in a range of development environments.
sections.plainLanguage: Sessions are tracked using a cookie, like a ticket. When the equipment and client talk, they exchange a ticket number in HTTP headers to remember which conversation is which. Memory constraints matter on network gear, so simpler is better.

layers.label: NETCONF Application
layers.detail: Client sends commands or server receives configuration requests

layers.label: Generated Java Stubs
layers.detail: Automatically generated from WSDL files, translates operations to SOAP messages

layers.label: SOAP Implementation
layers.detail: Apache Axis or similar, handles XML parsing and envelope construction
